title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise.
authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, Fatouros IG, Kyparos A, Nikolaidis MG, Paschalis V.
journal: Scandinavian journal of medicine & science in sports
abstract: The duration of the repeated-bout effect following eccentric knee-extensor exercise remains undefined, despite its widespread use in muscle damage research and training. The present study examined how long this protective effect persists in the knee extensors. Forty-eight young men performed two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 × 15 repetitions at 60°/s). Four independent groups performed the second bout 3, 6, 9, or 12 weeks after the first. Isometric torque, range of motion (ROM), delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), muscle thickness, echo intensity, creatine kinase (CK), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) were assessed before and 2 and 4 days after each bout. Baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models were used to compare responses between bouts, complemented by equivalence testing at 12 weeks. The repeated-bout effect was evident at 3 and 6 weeks across most outcomes and remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers. At 12 weeks, no significant differences between bouts were observed at either day 2 or day 4 for any outcome. Exploratory equivalence analyses further indicated that the effect was no longer meaningfully present at these time points for isometric torque, ROM, DOMS, muscle thickness, and echo intensity, whereas the findings for CK and hs-CRP remained inconclusive. Overall, the repeated-bout effect may persist for some outcomes for up to 9 weeks, whereas by 12 weeks no meaningful effect was detectable at the assessed post-exercise time points. This time course can guide the design of muscle damage studies and the scheduling of eccentric training sessions.

title: Can the cross-education of strength attenuate the impact of detraining after a period of strength training? A quasi-randomized trial.
authors: Rowe GS, Blazevich AJ, Taylor JL, Pulverenti T, Haff GG.
abstract: Purpose Unilateral strength training may attenuate the decline in muscle strength and size in homologous, contralateral muscles. This study aimed to determine whether the cross-education of strength could specifically attenuate the effects of detraining immediately after a short (prehabilitation-type) period of strength training. Methods Twenty-six strength-trained participants were assigned to either four weeks of unilateral strength training of the stronger arm (UNI) or detraining (Detrain). Motor evoked potential (MEP) and cortical silent period (cSP) responses, muscle cross-sectional area (CSA Flexor ; peripheral quantitative computed tomography) and maximal strength, rate of force development (RFD) and muscle activation (EMG) were examined in both elbow flexors before and after the intervention period. Results In UNI, one-repetition maximum (1-RM) strength improved in both the trained (∆ = 2.0 ± 0.9 kg) and non-trained (∆ = 0.8 ± 0.9 kg) arms despite cessation of training of the weaker arm, whereas 1-RM strength was unchanged in Detrain. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, isokinetic peak torque, and RFD did not change in either group. No neural changes were detected in UNI, but cSP increased in Detrain (∆ = 0.010 ± 0.015 s). CSA Flexor increased in the trained arm (∆ = 51 ± 43 mm 2 ) but decreased in the non-trained arm (∆ = -53 ± 50 mm 2 ) in UNI. CSA Flexor decreased in both arms in Detrain and at a similar rate to the non-trained arm in UNI. Conclusion UNI attenuated the effects of detraining in the weaker arm as shown by the improvement in 1-RM strength. However, the cross-education of strength did not attenuate the decline in muscle size in the contralateral arm.

title: Physiological, Perceptual, and Performance Responses to the 2-Week Block of High- versus Low-Intensity Endurance Training.
authors: Nuuttila OP, Nummela A, Kyröläinen H, Laukkanen J, Häkkinen K.
journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
abstract: Purpose This study examined the physiological, perceptual, and performance responses to a 2-wk block of increased training load and compared whether responses differ between high-intensity interval (HIIT) and low-intensity training (LIT). Methods Thirty recreationally trained males and females performed a 2-wk block of 10 HIIT sessions (INT, n = 15) or 70% increased volume of LIT (VOL, n = 15). Running time in the 3000 m and basal serum and urine hormone concentrations were measured before (T1) and after the block (T2), and after a recovery week (T3). In addition, weekly averages of nocturnal heart rate variability (HRV) and perceived recovery were compared with the baseline. Results Both groups improved their running time in the 3000 m from T1 to T2 (INT = -1.8% ± 1.6%, P = 0.003; VOL = -1.4% ± 1.7%, P = 0.017) and from T1 to T3 (INT = -2.5% ± 1.6%, P Conclusions HIIT and LIT blocks increased endurance performance in a short period. Although both protocols seemed to be tolerable for recreational athletes, a HIIT block may induce some negative responses such as increased muscle soreness and decreased parasympathetic activity.
